script:
export const meta = {
  name: 'dev-seed-research',
  description: 'Survey genuinely public-domain content sources for fit with Lucifer\'s Diary (modern literary erotica), inventory the project\'s existing tag-seed pattern + dependencies, and draft a complete synthetic Prisma seed script — return a decision menu (PD-content vs synthetic) with both ready to execute.',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Research', detail: 'parallel: PD-source survey, project inventory, synthetic seed plan draft' },
    { title: 'Synthesis', detail: 'consolidated decision menu with both options costed out' },
  ],
}

const PD_SURVEY_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  properties: {
    sources: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        additionalProperties: false,
        properties: {
          name: { type: 'string' },
          url: { type: 'string' },
          legalStatus: { type: 'string', description: 'Confirmed PD? CC0? CC-BY-NC? Verified or claimed?' },
          approximateRelevantVolume: { type: 'string', description: 'Rough count of works in the literary-erotica / sensual-prose category' },
          era: { type: 'string', description: 'Era of available works (Victorian / Renaissance / Modern / etc)' },
          voiceFit: { type: 'string', description: 'Honest assessment of fit with a modern slow-burn-literary-erotica site' },
          tagFit: { type: 'string', description: 'Would the existing 591-tag taxonomy of Lucifer\'s Diary map onto this content?' },
        },
        required: ['name', 'url', 'legalStatus', 'approximateRelevantVolume', 'era', 'voiceFit', 'tagFit'],
      },
    },
    modernPDExists: { type: 'string', description: 'Honest answer: is there a usable pool of CC0 / verified-PD MODERN erotic fiction online?' },
    overallVerdict: { type: 'string', description: 'Plain-English assessment of whether PD content is a viable path for this use case' },
  },
  required: ['sources', 'modernPDExists', 'overallVerdict'],
}

const PROJECT_INVENTORY_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  properties: {
    tagSeedScript: { type: 'string', description: 'Path + pattern of the existing tag-seeding script' },
    tagCount: { type: 'integer', description: 'Total tags currently in the taxonomy' },
    adultTagCount: { type: 'integer' },
    fakerInstalled: { type: 'boolean' },
    fakerVersion: { type: 'string' },
    prismaVersion: { type: 'string' },
    seedScriptConvention: { type: 'string', description: 'How existing scripts in backend/scripts/ are structured + invoked' },
    schemaShapeNotes: { type: 'string', description: 'Required fields on Story / Chapter / Series for an insert' },
  },
  required: ['tagSeedScript', 'tagCount', 'fakerInstalled', 'seedScriptConvention', 'schemaShapeNotes'],
}

const SYNTHETIC_PLAN_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  properties: {
    filePath: { type: 'string' },
    cliArgs: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    safetyGuards: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    contentVolume: { type: 'object', additionalProperties: false, properties: {
      stories: { type: 'integer' },
      series: { type: 'integer' },
      chaptersPerSeries: { type: 'string' },
      totalChapters: { type: 'integer' },
    }, required: ['stories', 'series', 'chaptersPerSeries', 'totalChapters'] },
    markerStrategy: { type: 'string', description: 'How seeded rows are tagged so --purge can find them' },
    purgeLogic: { type: 'string' },
    titleGenerationApproach: { type: 'string', description: 'How realistic-but-non-copyrighted titles are generated' },
    excerptGenerationApproach: { type: 'string' },
    bodyGenerationApproach: { type: 'string' },
    tagSelectionAlgorithm: { type: 'string' },
    codeSkeleton: { type: 'string', description: 'Real TypeScript skeleton (~150-250 lines) showing the script\'s actual structure' },
  },
  required: ['filePath', 'cliArgs', 'safetyGuards', 'contentVolume', 'markerStrategy', 'purgeLogic', 'codeSkeleton'],
}

phase('Research')

const [pdSurvey, projectInventory, syntheticPlan] = await parallel([
  () => agent('Survey genuinely-public-domain content sources that could supply test fixtures for Lucifer\'s Diary, a modern literary erotica site. DO NOT scrape any content — ONLY produce metadata about sources (name, URL, volume, era, fit).\n\nSpecifically investigate:\n1. Project Gutenberg — search their catalog (via WebFetch / WebSearch) for the categories most relevant: "Erotic fiction", "Erotica", "Sex", "Romance" (classical-era only here), "Decameron" (Boccaccio), Casanova memoirs, "Fanny Hill" (Cleland, 1748), "My Secret Life" (anon, 1888), erotic poetry. For each: confirm Gutenberg lists it as Public Domain (their copyright header is authoritative), note the era, note the voice (Victorian / Classical / Renaissance vs modern).\n2. Standard Ebooks — they curate Gutenberg titles with modern editorial polish. Check if any sensual / romance / erotica titles are in their catalog.\n3. Wikisource — does any verified-PD erotica live there?\n4. Internet Archive — flag that "free to read" ≠ PD; most IA content is still in copyright. Be precise.\n5. CC0-tagged contemporary fiction collections — does ANY usable pool of modern CC0 / verified-PD erotica exist anywhere? Honest answer.\n\nReport via PD_SURVEY_SCHEMA. Be brutally honest about era / voice fit — a Victorian text on a contemporary literary-erotica site reads as wrong, and that\'s relevant to the user\'s actual decision.', { schema: PD_SURVEY_SCHEMA, label: 'pd-survey' }),

  () => agent('Inventory the existing Lucifer\'s Diary backend pieces relevant to building a new seed script. READ frontend/AGENTS.md context lives in the repo at /Users/taha/Claude projects/LucifersDiary — work from there.\n\nFind:\n1. The existing tag-seeding script (the README references `npm run seed:tags`). Read it: path, structure (top-level await? prisma client lifecycle? input data source?), how it\'s wired in backend/package.json scripts.\n2. The current count of tags in the taxonomy (parse docs/tag_taxonomy_3_tiers.md and/or docs/tag_extras.json). Split safe vs adult.\n3. backend/package.json — is @faker-js/faker installed? what version? what other relevant deps (prisma client, ts-node)?\n4. backend/prisma/schema.prisma — record the EXACT required fields for Story / Series / Chapter inserts (excluding auto-generated id/createdAt/updatedAt). Note relations to Tag via StoryTag / SeriesTag / ChapterTag join tables.\n5. The convention for running scripts in backend/scripts/ — are they .ts files? executed via ts-node? wired into npm scripts in package.json?\n\nReport via PROJECT_INVENTORY_SCHEMA. Use Read + Grep extensively; cite exact line numbers where useful.', { schema: PROJECT_INVENTORY_SCHEMA, label: 'project-inventory' }),

  () => agent('Draft a COMPLETE plan for backend/scripts/seed-dev-content.ts — a synthetic Prisma seed script that materializes 50 stories + 8 series (with 3-8 chapters each) for dev-only stress-testing of the recently-shipped GSAP animations (PRs #187–#191) on Lucifer\'s Diary.\n\nRequirements:\n\nVOLUME: 50 standalone Story rows, 8 Series rows with 3-8 chapters each (so ~40-60 total chapters).\n\nSAFETY GUARDS (non-negotiable):\n- Requires explicit `--confirm=dev` CLI flag; running without it prints a warning and exits with code 1.\n- Requires `LUCIFER_ENV=dev` env var to be set. Without it the script refuses to run.\n- Each seeded row is marked with a discoverable token (recommend: in a dedicated field if one exists, or as a known prefix like `[seed-dev]` in the title — pick the cleaner option based on schema).\n- Idempotent: rerunning the script does NOT duplicate rows. Either detects existing seed rows (by marker) and refuses, or skips them.\n- Supports `--purge` flag that wipes ONLY rows matching the marker (no other rows touched).\n- Supports `--dry-run` flag that prints exactly what WOULD insert (counts + first few titles) without actually writing to the DB.\n\nCONTENT GENERATION (the key constraint: no copyrighted material reproduced anywhere):\n- Titles: faker-driven with a literary-evocative twist. Approach: combine word-pools from faker.word.* with hand-curated mood words (suggestive but not explicit) — e.g. `${faker.word.adjective()} ${moodNoun}` or `The ${noun} of ${faker.person.firstName()}`. Output should sound brand-appropriate (think evocative literary titles, not graphic).\n- Excerpts: faker.lorem.sentences(3) modified to sound moody — prepend with one of a small pool of evocative openers. 100% original (faker-generated), not derived from any source.\n- Bodies: pure faker.lorem.paragraphs() — varied length from ~500 to ~10,000 words. Animation testing doesn\'t care what the body says, only how long it is.\n- Tags: read the existing tag taxonomy from the DB at script-runtime via prisma.tag.findMany(), pick 3-6 random tags per row weighted to include both safe and adult tags. Mix should match real-site distribution roughly.\n- isAuthorsChoice: 5% probability per story/chapter.\n- publishedAt: spread across the last 6 months, random.\n- Series.status: weighted mix of ONGOING / COMPLETE / HIATUS.\n- estimatedReadMinutes: computed from body word count.\n\nReport via SYNTHETIC_PLAN_SCHEMA. The codeSkeleton field should be a real TypeScript draft (~150-250 lines) showing argument parsing, env-guard, prisma lifecycle, content generators, tag-selection algorithm, marker logic, purge logic, dry-run logic — enough to commit and refine, not pseudo-code. Use the project-inventory findings (faker version, schema shape, script convention) — the synthesizer agent will pass them in via context.', { schema: SYNTHETIC_PLAN_SCHEMA, label: 'synthetic-plan' }),
])

log('Research complete. Synthesizing decision menu.')

phase('Synthesis')

const decision = await agent(
  'Synthesize a decision menu for the user comparing two options for populating their dev database with test content. The user has been pushing for "real content from non-copyrighted sources" — your job is to put genuine survey data + the synthetic alternative side by side so they can make a clear call.\n\n' +
  'INPUTS:\n\n' +
  'PD SURVEY: ' + JSON.stringify(pdSurvey) + '\n\n' +
  'PROJECT INVENTORY: ' + JSON.stringify(projectInventory) + '\n\n' +
  'SYNTHETIC PLAN: ' + JSON.stringify(syntheticPlan) + '\n\n' +
  'Output a JSON object with these fields:\n' +
  '- summary: 2-3 sentences capturing the headline finding (e.g. "PD pool exists but it\'s X works, Y era, Z fit — synthetic is more aligned with the test goal").\n' +
  '- pdOption: { viable: boolean, volume: string, voiceFit: string, fitForGSAPTesting: string, recommendation: "use" | "skip" | "use-some" }. Be honest.\n' +
  '- syntheticOption: { fileSummary: string, volumeSummary: string, safetySummary: string, runCommand: string, purgeCommand: string }.\n' +
  '- recommendation: "synthetic" | "pd-only" | "hybrid" — your single best call, with one sentence of why.\n' +
  '- readyToBuild: boolean — is the synthetic plan complete enough that a "yes, build" lands the script in develop within one focused PR? (Should be true.)\n' +
  '- whatBuildLooksLike: 4-6 bullet points describing the actual PR scope (files created/modified, what the user runs after merge).\n' +
  '- openQuestionsForUser: list of any genuine decisions the user still needs to make (be brief — only items that change the build).',
  {
    schema: {
      type: 'object',
      additionalProperties: false,
      properties: {
        summary: { type: 'string' },
        pdOption: { type: 'object', additionalProperties: false, properties: {
          viable: { type: 'boolean' },
          volume: { type: 'string' },
          voiceFit: { type: 'string' },
          fitForGSAPTesting: { type: 'string' },
          recommendation: { type: 'string' },
        }, required: ['viable', 'volume', 'voiceFit', 'fitForGSAPTesting', 'recommendation'] },
        syntheticOption: { type: 'object', additionalProperties: false, properties: {
          fileSummary: { type: 'string' },
          volumeSummary: { type: 'string' },
          safetySummary: { type: 'string' },
          runCommand: { type: 'string' },
          purgeCommand: { type: 'string' },
        }, required: ['fileSummary', 'volumeSummary', 'safetySummary', 'runCommand', 'purgeCommand'] },
        recommendation: { type: 'string' },
        readyToBuild: { type: 'boolean' },
        whatBuildLooksLike: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
        openQuestionsForUser: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
      },
      required: ['summary', 'pdOption', 'syntheticOption', 'recommendation', 'readyToBuild', 'whatBuildLooksLike'],
    },
    label: 'synthesize',
  }
)

return {
  pdSurvey,
  projectInventory,
  syntheticPlan,
  decision,
}

sources.name: Project Gutenberg — Erotic Fiction bookshelf (#33)
sources.legalStatus: Verified Public Domain in US. Project Gutenberg's standard PG license header is authoritative — every title carries an explicit PD declaration. Note: PD-in-US ≠ PD globally; some titles still under copyright in EU/UK.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: ~16 titles total in the dedicated Erotic Fiction bookshelf, of which only ~10-12 are literary erotica (the rest are reference/manuals like Kama Sutra, or non-English). Realistically 5-8 English-language literary-erotica titles usable: Fanny Hill (1748), Venus in Furs (1870), Decameron (1350s, 2 vols), Erotica Romana / Roman Elegies (Goethe, late 1700s), Aline et Valcour (Sade, French only).
sources.era: Almost entirely pre-1900. Oldest: Petronius's Satyricon (1st century CE) and Decameron (14th century). Most recent: Ulysses (1922, modernist — borderline). Median is mid-1700s to late-1800s.
sources.voiceFit: Brutally honest: BAD fit for a modern slow-burn literary-erotica site. Fanny Hill's voice — 'I was now reduced to such a state of distress... that the velvet-soft pressure of his glowing instrument...' — is florid 18th-century euphemism. Venus in Furs is German philosophical-fetishist 1870s prose. Decameron is medieval frame-narrative bawdy. NONE of these read as contemporary literary-erotica voice (think Garth Greenwell, Mary Gaitskill, Melissa Febos). Use as historical curiosity only — never as a default sample for a contemporary site.
sources.tagFit: Poor. A 591-tag modern taxonomy almost certainly includes tags like 'consent-forward,' 'queer contemporary,' 'praise kink,' 'aftercare,' 'dom/sub dynamics with modern negotiation,' 'monogamish,' etc. The PG corpus pre-dates the entire vocabulary of modern kink-and-consent discourse. Tags that would map: gender-coded acts, fetish (Sacher-Masoch → masochism literally), maybe orientalist exotica. Tags that would NOT map: anything post-1970s sexual-politics vocabulary, anything queer-affirming, anything with modern consent framing. You'd be force-fitting.

sources.name: Project Gutenberg — Sexuality & Erotica bookshelf (#703)
sources.legalStatus: Verified Public Domain in US (PG header authoritative).
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: 25+ titles across 2+ pages. Mix of literary erotica (Sade, Sacher-Masoch, Cleland, Frank Harris's My Life and Loves) and clinical/scientific texts (Freud, Havelock Ellis, Searchlights on Health — a Victorian sex-hygiene manual). The literary-erotica subset is perhaps 8-12 titles.
sources.era: Same Victorian-to-Edwardian skew as #33, plus early-20th-century clinical/Freud material.
sources.voiceFit: Worse than #33 if anything — Frank Harris's My Life and Loves (1922-27) is closest to 'modern' but reads as Edwardian boastful memoir, not literary erotica. Freud and Havelock Ellis are not fiction at all — they're medico-sexological treatises. Including these in a modern erotica site's fixtures would be a category error.
sources.tagFit: Poor for fiction tagging; some clinical texts might supply 'sexuality discourse' fixtures but that's a different product than Lucifer's Diary.

sources.name: Project Gutenberg — Casanova: Histoire de ma vie (Memoirs of Jacques Casanova)
sources.legalStatus: Public Domain in US (PG-hosted, Arthur Machen 1894 translation). The Machen translation itself is PD because >95 years old. WARNING: the unabridged 1966-71 Willard Trask translation is STILL in copyright — only the bowdlerized Machen version is freely usable.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: 1 work, ~12 volumes, very long. Sex scenes are scattered through memoir-style prose, not the bulk of the text.
sources.era: Written 1789-98, translated 1894. Voice is Enlightenment-era libertine memoir filtered through late-Victorian English.
sources.voiceFit: Mixed. Casanova has genuine narrative momentum and psychological texture other PG erotica lacks, but the Machen translation is censored — the actual sex is mostly elided or euphemized. So the corpus you can legally use lacks the explicit content that would make it useful as erotica fixtures in the first place. The unabridged version that contains the actual erotic content is NOT public domain.
sources.tagFit: Some overlap with modern 'rake/seducer/multi-partner' tags but framed as 18th-century libertinage. Modern consent vocabulary entirely absent.

sources.name: Standard Ebooks
sources.legalStatus: Curates only verified-PD works (sources from PG and verifies independently). Their editorial standard is high — modern typography, corrected typos, consistent style.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: ZERO dedicated erotica titles. A 'romance' keyword search returns ~12-30 titles, but these are Romance-as-genre (Conrad/Ford's Romance, Lorna Doone, Prince Otto) — adventure-romance, not erotic or sensual fiction. Standard Ebooks does not curate the Fanny Hill / Sade / Sacher-Masoch line at all.
sources.era: Their catalog skews 19th and early-20th-century literary canon — Austen, Dickens, James, Wharton, Conrad.
sources.voiceFit: Their editorial polish is great, but they don't have the source material. Even Austen/Wharton — closest to 'literary, restrained sensuality' — are emphatically NOT erotica. Useless as a direct source for erotica fixtures.
sources.tagFit: N/A — no erotica corpus to tag.

sources.name: Wikisource — Category:Erotica
sources.legalStatus: PD via {{PD-US}} template (published before 1931). Each work's PD status is individually templated and verifiable.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: ~24 pages in the category, including subcategories (erotic poetry: 9, sex manuals: 5, pornographic film: 4). The literary fiction subset overlaps heavily with PG plus a few Victorian-clandestine additions: The Pearl (Victorian periodical, ~1879-1880), The Romance of Lust (1873), Teleny (attrib. Wilde, 1893), Autobiography of a Flea (1887), Venus in India, A Night in a Moorish Harem, The Way of a Man with a Maid. Maybe 8-10 unique titles not on PG.
sources.era: Almost entirely Victorian clandestine erotica (1870s-1900s). Tiny amount of early-20th-century.
sources.voiceFit: Victorian clandestine erotica has a very recognizable voice — heavy use of period-specific euphemism ('the altar of Venus,' 'his weapon,' 'her secret place'), highly mechanical descriptions, often racist and colonialist (Venus in India, Moorish Harem). For a contemporary literary-erotica fixture pool this voice is actively HARMFUL — it would train any UI text-mocking, recommendation, or tag-display feature on language that contemporary readers would find either laughable or offensive. Teleny is the one partial exception (often attributed to Oscar Wilde's circle, queer literary, slightly more elevated prose) but still Victorian.
sources.tagFit: Very poor for modern taxonomy. The Pearl etc. contain a lot of incest/non-consent/colonial-fetish content that maps to modern tags ONLY in disturbing ways. Tagging fidelity would be low and ethically fraught.

sources.name: Internet Archive (general collection)
sources.legalStatus: MIXED and dangerous to assume. IA explicitly states: 'The Internet Archive does not make guarantees as to the copyright status of items on archive.org.' 'Free to read' / 'borrowable' / 'streamable' is NOT public domain — most modern IA content is in-copyright and made available under contested Controlled Digital Lending (which lost in Hachette v. Internet Archive, 2023). PD content on IA is the items SOURCED from PG, HathiTrust, government, or with explicit CC0/PD tags. Erotica that's actually PD on IA = essentially the same PG/Wikisource set, mirrored.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: If you filter to verified PD (e.g., items sourced from Project Gutenberg or with explicit PD/CC0 metadata), the relevant erotic-fiction set is essentially identical to the PG bookshelf — no real expansion. Anything else labeled 'free to read' is in-copyright and legally unsafe for fixtures.
sources.era: PD subset same as PG (pre-1930). Non-PD subset spans everything.
sources.voiceFit: Same as PG for the legally-usable portion. The temptation to grab modern erotica 'free to read' on IA is the trap — that content is in copyright and using it as fixtures exposes Lucifer's Diary to takedown/DMCA risk.

sources.name: The Public Domain Review
sources.legalStatus: Curated PD work with editorial essays. PDR vets PD status carefully.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: Tiny — single-digit curated essays/items tagged erotica (The Book of Exposition: 15th-century Middle Eastern erotica 1900 ed.; Harris's List of Covent-Garden Ladies 1757-95; pseudo-Boccaccio pieces). Curated, not a corpus.
sources.voiceFit: PDR's mission is precisely 'curious historical artifacts' — its erotica tag is for cultural-history readers, not as a content pool. Voice fit zero for modern site.

sources.name: CC0 / verified-PD MODERN erotica corpora
sources.legalStatus: Effectively does not exist as a meaningful pool. CC0 requires the rights-holder to explicitly waive copyright; no significant body of contemporary erotica authors has done so. Spot-check searches across CC0 indexes (Creative Commons, getfreeebooks CC0 lists, Wikipedia CC0 works) return zero modern literary-erotica collections. The few 'free' modern erotica corpora online are either author-promo (still copyrighted, just gratis) or pirated.
sources.approximateRelevantVolume: Zero meaningful volume. Maybe a handful of individual short pieces on personal blogs/Wattpad under CC0, but no curated corpus, no editorial vetting, no scale.
sources.voiceFit: Would be the ONLY voice-appropriate source if it existed — but it doesn't.
sources.tagFit: Would map cleanly to the 591-tag taxonomy if a corpus existed — but no such corpus exists.

pdSurvey.modernPDExists: No. There is no usable pool of CC0 or verified-public-domain MODERN erotic fiction online. After surveying Creative Commons indexes, Project Gutenberg post-1929 holdings, Standard Ebooks, Wikisource, Internet Archive, and Public Domain Review, the available verified-PD corpus is overwhelmingly pre-1930 (most of it pre-1900), with voice and tag vocabularies that do not match a contemporary literary-erotica site. Contemporary authors essentially never release erotica under CC0 — the genre's economics (paid platforms, Patreon, indie publishing) and stigma both push the opposite direction. The 'modern free erotica' that exists online is either (a) author-promo content still under copyright, (b) Controlled-Digital-Lending material on IA that is legally contested and NOT public domain, or (c) unlicensed/pirated. None of these are safe as fixture sources.
pdSurvey.overallVerdict: PD content is NOT a viable path for Lucifer's Diary fixtures if the goal is voice-representative test data. The honest landscape: roughly 15-25 unique English-language literary-erotica works are reliably PD (Fanny Hill, Venus in Furs, Decameron, Casanova/Machen, Teleny, The Pearl, Romance of Lust, My Secret Life, Sade selections, Frank Harris, Autobiography of a Flea, plus a handful of erotic poetry — Sappho, Catullus, Goethe's Roman Elegies). Every single one is pre-1930, most are Victorian or earlier, and they share three disqualifying traits for a modern slow-burn-literary-erotica fixture pool: (1) florid period-specific euphemism that reads as parody to contemporary eyes, (2) consent and sexual-politics vocabularies that are absent or actively offensive (colonial fetish, racism, non-consent framed as titillation), and (3) tag-taxonomy mismatch — a 591-tag modern system built around contemporary kink/identity/consent discourse cannot meaningfully tag Victorian clandestine prose without force-fitting. Three practical paths forward, ranked: (1) BEST: commission a small (~20-50 piece) original fixture corpus from a freelance erotica writer with a work-for-hire / CC0 release — gives voice fidelity, tag fidelity, and unambiguous license. (2) ACCEPTABLE: generate synthetic fixture text with an LLM specifically for fixture-display purposes (clearly labeled as synthetic, not as real content). (3) WORST but cheapest: use the PG corpus for STRUCTURAL fixtures only (chapter counts, word counts, tag density) without ever surfacing the actual prose in UI. Do NOT mix Victorian PD prose into anything a real user would see — it will undermine the contemporary brand. The Standard Ebooks 'we curate PD with editorial polish' model is not a shortcut here because they correctly don't curate erotica. Internet Archive's 'free to read' is a copyright trap, not a source. CC0 modern erotica is essentially a null set.

projectInventory.tagSeedScript: backend/scripts/seed-tags.ts — standalone TS file. Wired in backend/package.json line 23: "seed:tags": "ts-node --transpile-only scripts/seed-tags.ts". Pattern: imports PrismaClient directly, parses docs/tag_taxonomy_3_tiers.md (Tier 1 -> isAdult=false, Tier 2/3 -> isAdult=true), merges docs/tag_extras.json (last-write-wins by lower-cased name), then loops with prisma.tag.findUnique + create/update (idempotent on name). Uses slugify from src/common/utils/slug.ts plus a local uniqueSlug() helper. Lifecycle: new PrismaClient() then try { ... } finally { prisma.$disconnect() }. main().catch(err => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); }) at module bottom. Runs from /backend with: npm run seed:tags.
projectInventory.fakerVersion: not installed — no @faker-js/faker in backend/package.json deps or devDeps, and no node_modules/@faker-js directory. Would need `npm i -D @faker-js/faker` in backend/.
projectInventory.prismaVersion: @prisma/client ^6.19.3 (prod dep), prisma ^6.19.3 (prod dep, used for migrate). ts-node ^10.9.2 (dev). typescript ^5.7.3 (dev). @types/node ^24.0.0 (dev). tsconfig-paths ^4.2.0 (dev) available for path aliases.
projectInventory.seedScriptConvention: Scripts live at backend/scripts/*.ts (sibling of src/, prisma/). Run via ts-node --transpile-only (skips full type-check). Each is wired into backend/package.json scripts under the seed:* namespace and invoked with `npm run seed:<name>` from the backend/ directory. Two existing patterns: (1) direct Prisma — seed-tags.ts instantiates PrismaClient, does idempotent upserts, calls prisma.$disconnect() in a finally block; (2) live admin API — seed-content.ts loads backend/.env via dotenv.config({path: resolve(__dirname,'..','.env')}), POSTs to /auth/login for a JWT, then hits /admin/* endpoints with native fetch (Node 18+). The API pattern requires the dev server running on localhost:3001 and ADMIN_PASSWORD set in backend/.env, and exercises the real publish path. Both end with main().catch(err => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); }). Both are idempotent — tags upsert on name, stories/series skip-if-title-exists, chapters skip-if-title-exists-within-series.
projectInventory.schemaShapeNotes:
Required fields for a direct Prisma insert (excluding id/createdAt/updatedAt and columns with defaults):

Story (schema.prisma:43-80):
- REQUIRED: title (String), content (String), excerpt (String), estimatedReadMinutes (Int).
- Has defaults: accumulatedReadSeconds (BigInt, 0), likeCount (Int, 0), isAuthorsChoice (Boolean, false).
- Optional/nullable: epigraph, authorsNote, publishedAt (set to make public; null = draft), deletedAt.
- Do NOT write: searchVector (Postgres-generated tsvector; Unsupported type).
- Tags via join table StoryTag { storyId, tagId } — composite PK, no extra columns. Nest-create with `tags: { create: tagIds.map(tagId => ({ tagId })) }`.
- notes is a Note[] relation (replaces legacy `notes` string column). Optional.

Series (schema.prisma:86-116):
- REQUIRED: title (String), excerpt (String).
- Has defaults: status (SeriesStatus enum: ONGOING|COMPLETE|HIATUS, default ONGOING), accumulatedReadSeconds, likeCount.
- Optional/nullable: authorsNote, deletedAt.
- Series has NO publishedAt (publish state lives on chapters).
- Tags via SeriesTag { seriesId, tagId } — composite PK.
- Do NOT write: searchVector.

Chapter (schema.prisma:128-161):
- REQUIRED: seriesId (FK -> Series.id), title (String), content (String), excerpt (String), orderIndex (Int — manual, no default; pick max+1 per series), estimatedReadMinutes (Int).
- Has defaults: isAuthorsChoice (false), accumulatedReadSeconds (0), likeCount (0).
- Optional/nullable: epigraph, authorsNote, publishedAt (null = draft), deletedAt.
- Tags via ChapterTag { chapterId, tagId } — composite PK.
- Do NOT write: searchVector.

If seeding via the admin API instead (mirrors seed-content.ts):
- POST /admin/stories (CreateStoryDto, backend/src/stories/dto/create-story.dto.ts): required title, content, excerpt, estimatedReadMinutes; optional isAuthorsChoice, authorsNote, epigraph, tagIds (UUID[]). Then PATCH /admin/stories/:id/publish to publish.
- POST /admin/series (CreateSeriesDto): required title, excerpt; optional authorsNote, status (SeriesStatus), tagIds.
- POST /admin/series/:seriesId/chapters (CreateChapterDto): required title, content, excerpt, estimatedReadMinutes; optional isAuthorsChoice, authorsNote, epigraph, tagIds. orderIndex is NOT in the DTO — assigned server-side. Then PATCH /admin/chapters/:id/publish to publish.

cliArgs: --confirm=dev (required; without it the script prints a warning + exits 1)
--purge (deletes ONLY rows whose title starts with the [seed-dev] marker; mutually exclusive with seeding)
--dry-run (prints counts + first 5 titles per type that would insert, no DB writes)
--seed=<int> (optional faker seed for reproducible runs; default = Date.now())
safetyGuards: Hard env-guard: refuses to run unless process.env.LUCIFER_ENV === 'dev'. Logs the actual value seen + exits 1.

Defensive DATABASE_URL check: if the URL contains 'prod', 'production', 'render.com', 'neon.tech', or any non-localhost host, abort with a loud red error before any write (extra belt-and-braces beyond LUCIFER_ENV).
Requires --confirm=dev. Without it, prints a 6-line warning explaining what the script does + that it writes garbage to the DB, then exits 1.

All seeded rows are tagged with the literal title prefix '[seed-dev] ' (Story.title, Series.title, Chapter.title). Cleaner than adding a schema column for a dev-only concern; survives every Prisma query as a plain string and is trivially LIKE-searchable.

Idempotent re-runs: before inserting, the script counts existing rows whose title starts with '[seed-dev] '. If count > 0 and --purge wasn't passed, it refuses to seed and tells the user to run --purge first (avoids the 'I ran it twice and now I have 100 stories' footgun).

--purge only deletes rows matching `title startsWith '[seed-dev] '`. Uses prisma.story.deleteMany({ where: { title: { startsWith: '[seed-dev] ' } } }) — junction tables (StoryTag/SeriesTag/ChapterTag) and Notes cascade via existing onDelete: Cascade. Chapters cascade when their Series is deleted.
--dry-run short-circuits before every prisma write. Each generator function still runs (so titles + counts are real), but the prisma.$transaction call is skipped and we log the plan instead.

Single top-level prisma.$transaction wraps every insert so a mid-script crash leaves zero partial rows. The transaction timeout is bumped to 120_000 ms because 50+ stories × up-to-10k-word bodies can be slow on a cold local DB.
Process exit codes are strict: 0 success, 1 guard failure, 2 mid-run runtime error. Lets CI / pre-commit hooks distinguish 'you ran it wrong' from 'the DB is broken'.
All console output is prefixed with '[seed-dev]' so it's grep-able in a busy terminal.

contentVolume.chaptersPerSeries: random integer in [3, 8] inclusive, drawn per-series via faker.number.int({ min: 3, max: 8 }) — empirically averages 5.5, so ~44 chapters across 8 series (within the requested 40–60 envelope)

syntheticPlan.markerStrategy: Title prefix '[seed-dev] ' on every Story, Series, and Chapter. Chosen over a dedicated schema column because (a) it requires zero migration, (b) it's visible to a human poking at the DB without reading code, (c) Prisma's `startsWith` filter makes purge a one-liner, and (d) it gracefully no-ops if the marker convention is ever changed (old rows stay discoverable). The prefix is exported as a top-level const SEED_MARKER = '[seed-dev] ' so the seed and purge paths can never drift.
syntheticPlan.purgeLogic: "On --purge, run inside a single prisma.$transaction: (1) delete all Chapter rows whose seriesId belongs to a Series with title startsWith SEED_MARKER (Prisma can't startsWith-filter across relations in deleteMany, so do this in two steps: findMany the matching series ids, then deleteMany chapters where seriesId in those ids), (2) delete all Series rows with title startsWith SEED_MARKER (cascades remaining chapters + SeriesTag rows + Follow rows), (3) delete all Story rows with title startsWith SEED_MARKER (cascades StoryTag + Note rows). Likes / ReadSessions / ReadingPositions / SavedContent are polymorphic with no FK — but a fresh dev DB won't have any pointing at seed rows, and the script logs a one-line warning telling the operator to manually clean those tables if they've been populated. Print a summary line: '[seed-dev] purged: N stories, M series, K chapters'. Exit 0."
syntheticPlan.tagSelectionAlgorithm: "At script start, prisma.tag.findMany() pulls the full taxonomy once and splits it into safeTags (isAdult=false) and adultTags (isAdult=true). For each story / series / chapter, pick a count in [3, 6] via faker.number.int. Then for each pick, with probability 0.7 draw from safeTags else from adultTags — this mirrors the rough real-site distribution (most content is Tier-1-only with an occasional Tier-2/3 dusting). Use a Set to dedupe so a row can't pick the same tag twice. If the DB has fewer than 6 tags in either bucket, gracefully clamp to whatever's available and log a one-time warning. Build the join rows via the createMany inside the same transaction (StoryTag / SeriesTag / ChapterTag), not via nested writes, to avoid 50 round-trips."
syntheticPlan.titleGenerationApproach: "Hand-curated mood-word pools (MOOD_NOUNS ~30 entries like 'Lamplight', 'Threshold', 'Hollow', 'Cinder', 'Drawer', 'Bell', 'Mourning', 'Letter'; MOOD_ADJS ~25 entries like 'Borrowed', 'Hollow', 'Quiet', 'Brittle', 'Late', 'Soft', 'Forgotten') combined via 4 rotating templates: (1) `The ${MOOD_NOUN} of ${faker.person.firstName()}`, (2) `${MOOD_ADJ} ${MOOD_NOUN}`, (3) `${faker.word.adjective()} ${MOOD_NOUN}` with the faker word title-cased, (4) `After ${MOOD_NOUN}`. Template chosen per row by faker.helpers.arrayElement. Result feels brand-aligned (echoes the existing 'On Lamplight', 'Borrowed Mornings', 'Hollow Sundays' tone) without literally copying any extant title — every word is either faker-generated or from a 100% original hand-pool. Final output is `${SEED_MARKER}${generatedTitle}`. Collision-resistant: appends a numeric suffix '(2)', '(3)'… if a freshly-generated title already exists in the in-script Set of generated titles."
syntheticPlan.excerptGenerationApproach: "faker.lorem.sentences(3) for the bulk, prefixed with one of an EVOCATIVE_OPENERS pool (~12 entries like 'A meditation on', 'A small confession about', 'Some nights are', 'In the space between', 'A letter never sent about'). Result reads like a moody literary blurb and is 100% derived from faker output + the hand-pool — no source material involved. Excerpts cap at 240 chars (truncate on word boundary + add ellipsis) so they fit the existing UI."
syntheticPlan.bodyGenerationApproach: "For each row, pick a target word count via faker.number.int({ min: 500, max: 10000 }) — uniform distribution gives the GSAP scroll-animation test a healthy spread of short/medium/long bodies. Loop faker.lorem.paragraph({ min: 4, max: 9 }) sentences and join with double-newlines until accumulated word count >= target. The animation work in PRs #187–#191 cares about page length and scroll-distance, not semantics, so pure lorem is correct here. estimatedReadMinutes = Math.max(1, Math.round(wordCount / 220)) — 220 wpm is the project's established read-speed constant (matches what the live editor computes)."

decision.summary: The verified public-domain erotica pool is real but tiny (~15-25 unique English titles), almost entirely pre-1930, and reads as florid Victorian/Enlightenment euphemism with consent vocabularies that range from absent to actively offensive — using any of it in UI fixtures would actively undermine the contemporary slow-burn-literary brand. For the actual test goal (stressing GSAP scroll animations across PRs #187-#191, which care about page length and scroll distance, not prose semantics), a synthetic faker-driven seeder is both safer and more fit-for-purpose. The synthetic plan is fully spec'd, safety-guarded, idempotent, and ready to ship as a single PR.

pdOption.volume: ~15-25 unique English-language literary-erotica works total across PG bookshelves 33 + 703, Wikisource, and PDR. Modern CC0/PD erotica is effectively a null set. Anything on Internet Archive labeled 'free to read' that isn't sourced from PG is in-copyright and a DMCA trap.
pdOption.voiceFit: Bad. Every usable title is pre-1930, most are Victorian or earlier (Fanny Hill 1748, Venus in Furs 1870, Decameron 1350s, Teleny 1893, The Pearl 1879). Voice is florid period euphemism that reads as parody to contemporary eyes and clashes with the Garth-Greenwell/Mary-Gaitskill register the site is going for. Consent and queer-affirming vocabularies are absent; several titles (The Pearl, Venus in India, Moorish Harem) carry colonial-fetish and non-consent content that's ethically fraught to surface in any UI.
pdOption.fitForGSAPTesting: Mediocre even on the narrow technical goal. GSAP work cares about page length, scroll distance, and tag-density spread across stories/series/chapters — not prose authenticity. PD bodies exist (Decameron, Casanova/Machen) but ingestion, cleanup, and chunking into chapter-shaped units is meaningful engineering for content that you'd then have to hide from the UI anyway because it's brand-toxic. Synthetic lorem of controlled length hits the same animation surface with zero ingestion overhead.

syntheticOption.fileSummary: Single new file at backend/scripts/seed-dev-content.ts following the existing seed:* convention (sibling of seed-tags.ts and seed-content.ts, ts-node --transpile-only, idempotent main()/catch/disconnect lifecycle). Adds @faker-js/faker as a devDependency in backend/package.json and a `seed:dev` script entry. No schema migration — the [seed-dev] title prefix is the marker, so purge is a trivial startsWith filter.
syntheticOption.volumeSummary: 50 standalone stories + 8 series with 3-8 chapters each (averages ~44 chapters, within the 40-60 envelope). Each body is 500-10,000 words uniform-random to give the GSAP scroll work a healthy spread of short/medium/long pages. Tags pulled live from the DB's 591-tag taxonomy: 3-6 per row, 70/30 safe/adult mix so the distribution matches the rough real-site shape. Titles are hand-pooled mood words combined with faker — brand-aligned, never copied. Bodies are pure faker.lorem because animation work doesn't care about semantics.
syntheticOption.safetySummary: Three independent guards: (1) hard refuse unless LUCIFER_ENV=dev, (2) sniff DATABASE_URL for prod/production/render.com/neon.tech and abort if matched, (3) require --confirm=dev on every seed run. Idempotent — refuses to seed if [seed-dev] rows already exist, points operator at --purge. --purge wipes ONLY rows whose title starts with [seed-dev] (Story/Series/Chapter), inside a single transaction, with cascades handling junction tables. --dry-run prints counts + first 5 titles per type with zero writes. All inserts wrapped in one prisma.$transaction (120s timeout) so a mid-run crash leaves zero partial rows. Strict exit codes: 0 success, 1 guard failure, 2 runtime error.
syntheticOption.runCommand: cd backend && LUCIFER_ENV=dev npm run seed:dev -- --confirm=dev
syntheticOption.purgeCommand: cd backend && LUCIFER_ENV=dev npm run seed:dev -- --purge

openQuestionsForUser: Keep the default counts (50 stories / 8 series / 3-8 chapters each) or push higher for heavier scroll-stress?
Should the script also seed a handful of draft (publishedAt=null) rows so the admin draft views are exercised, or published-only as currently specced?
Lock in the [seed-dev] title prefix as the marker, or would you rather a less-visible tag (e.g. a specific authorsNote sentinel) so the prefix doesn't appear if a screenshot leaks?
